headline.title: Big Tech's AI spending hides $3T off the books.
headline.summary: A new WSJ report reveals that nine top tech firms carry $3 trillion in off-balance-sheet AI commitments, far exceeding what investors can see. This hidden financial exposure complicates assessments of tech giants' true obligations and risks.

stories.title: Big Tech's AI spending is $3T higher than it seems.
stories.toc_summary: WSJ finds nine tech giants have $3T in off-balance-sheet AI commitments, making true AI costs hard to gauge.
stories.quick_take: A WSJ investigation discovered that nine top tech firms are carrying $3 trillion in off-balance-sheet AI commitments, which are not reflected on their balance sheets [1]. These hidden obligations make it difficult for investors to assess each company's total AI spending and future liabilities [1]. The deals are growing larger and more complex, raising concerns about transparency and risk exposure [1].

bullets.label: Hidden obligations:
bullets.text: The WSJ found $3T in off-balance-sheet AI commitments across nine major tech companies, making their true AI spending appear much higher than reported [1].

bullets.label: Investor concern:
bullets.text: Investors have flagged that these deals are increasingly complex, making it harder to evaluate each firm's total financial commitments [1].

bullets.label: Scale insight:
bullets.text: This undisclosed spending dwarfs official capex figures, potentially reshaping how analysts model tech giants' financial health [1].

bullets.label: Trend watch:
bullets.text: With AI infrastructure deals ballooning, expect more scrutiny on off-balance-sheet financing in upcoming earnings calls [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: Investors and regulators need to push for clearer disclosure of AI-related financial commitments; otherwise, the market is flying blind on the true scale of Big Tech's AI bet.

stories.title: Slack Code turns coding into a group project.
stories.toc_summary: Slack's new feature brings AI coding agents into shared channels, letting teams collaborate on software builds together.
stories.quick_take: Slack launched Slack Code, a feature that lets teams develop software directly within messaging channels, where AI agents do the coding and humans steer, review, and approve [1]. Each 'code channel' brings together agents and users from different teams, with live previews for everyone [1]. Deployments require human approval, and finished projects leave archived channels as searchable records [1]. The feature is available on all Slack plans at launch, with AI agents like ChatGPT, Claude, Devin, Vercel, and GitHub available [1].

bullets.label: Collaborative coding:
bullets.text: Slack Code puts coding agents inside shared channels, enabling any team member to contribute to software builds, not just engineers [1].

bullets.label: Human oversight:
bullets.text: All changes require human approval before deployment, and completed projects leave searchable archives [1].

bullets.label: Agent choice:
bullets.text: Teams can connect agents like ChatGPT, Claude, Devin, Vercel, and GitHub to chat channels [1].

bullets.label: Accessibility:
bullets.text: Available to all Slack plans at launch, making AI-assisted development mainstream [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: The shift to AI-agent-enabled messaging builds is real, and Slack Code positions Slack as the venue where human-AI collaboration happens—an attempt to own the office space for the AI coworker era.

stories.title: OpenAI's Codex hits 20 million active users.
stories.toc_summary: OpenAI's coding agent Codex crossed 20 million weekly users, signaling the rise of AI-driven programming.
stories.quick_take: OpenAI's coding agent Codex surpassed 20 million active users this week, marking a major milestone in AI-assisted software development [1]. The company also credited each Codex and ChatGPT Work account with a 'banked reset'—an extra usage window that can be saved and used later [1]. This growth underscores the shift from manual coding to delegating to AI agents, with demand scaling faster than compute capacity [1].

bullets.label: User milestone:
bullets.text: Codex now has over 20 million active users, indicating widespread adoption [1].

bullets.label: Usage reset:
bullets.text: OpenAI is giving users a 'banked reset'—additional usage windows that can be saved and used when needed [1].

bullets.label: Programming shift:
bullets.text: Programming is moving from manual work at the editor to delegating to AI agents, changing the skills required [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: The rapid growth of Codex signals that AI-driven coding is becoming mainstream. Expect increased competition in AI coding agents and potential bottlenecks in compute capacity.

stories.title: Anthropic launches Claude Academy with 355 free resources.
stories.toc_summary: Anthropic's Claude Academy offers 355 tutorials and guides for free, aiming to become the standard AI learning platform.
stories.quick_take: Anthropic has launched the Claude Academy, a comprehensive learning hub with 355 free tutorials, prompting tips, and use-case examples [1][2]. The platform covers everything from beginner basics to advanced API usage, with two learning paths: one for interactive problem-solving and another for delegating tasks to Claude [1][2]. This move positions Claude as the go-to AI tool for a new generation of workers, making training and education a strategic advantage [2].

bullets.label: Free access:
bullets.text: All 355 resources are available at no cost and without a login requirement [1][2].

bullets.label: Skill levels:
bullets.text: Content ranges from beginner to expert, covering Claude, Cowork, Code, Tag, and the API [1].

bullets.label: Learning paths:
bullets.text: Two tracks: one for collaborative thinking and writing with Claude, another for task delegation [2].

bullets.label: Strategic move:
bullets.text: By offering free education, Anthropic aims to make Claude the standard tool for AI adoption in enterprises [2].

callout.label: LONG ARC
callout.text: Free education in AI is a strategic move to capture market share and build brand loyalty. Companies must decide which AI ecosystem to invest in as training becomes a key competitive factor.

stories.title: Generalist AI's robot learns from one demo.
stories.toc_summary: A robot arm learns new tasks from a single demonstration, hinting at a 'GPT-3 moment' for robotics.
stories.quick_take: Generalist AI's GEN-1.5 robot arm can learn a task from a single demonstration, without any training, using context like a language model [1]. In a test, it successfully moved a block to a bowl covered by a paper it had never seen before, then put the paper back [1]. This breakthrough could enable non-experts to program robots simply by showing them what to do [1].

bullets.label: One-shot learning:
bullets.text: GEN-1.5 learns a task from a few-second demo, without needing explicit training [1].

bullets.label: Adaptive behavior:
bullets.text: The robot handles novel obstacles, like a paper covering the bowl, by adjusting its actions [1].

bullets.label: Implications:
bullets.text: This could lower barriers to robot programming, making it accessible to non-engineers [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: This 'GPT-3 moment' for robotics means robots may soon be programmable by demonstration, potentially transforming industries where automation was previously too complex or costly.

stories.title: Galbot's ET1: Humanoid with a universal brain.
stories.toc_summary: Galbot unveils ET1 at World Robot Conference, a humanoid controlled by one World-Action Model across different robot bodies.
stories.quick_take: Chinese startup Galbot presented its first bipedal humanoid, ET1, at the World Robot Conference 2026 [1]. The key innovation is its 'World-Action Model' that controls both bipedal, wheeled, and heavy-load robots from a single brain [1]. Founded in 2023, Galbot is already planning a Hong Kong IPO with a valuation of $3-4 billion [1].

bullets.label: Universal control:
bullets.text: ET1 uses one world-action model to control various robot types, from bipedal to wheeled [1].

bullets.label: Fast growth:
bullets.text: Galbot's planned IPO at a $3-4B valuation shows rapid scaling in China's embodied AI sector [1].

bullets.label: Industry trend:
bullets.text: Chinese robotics startups are accelerating hardware releases weekly, outpacing Western debate [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: China's embodied AI scene is moving fast; watch for more startups following Galbot's path to IPO and the impact on global robotics competition.

editorial.title: The AI gold rush is becoming a data and compute race.
editorial.intro: Today's stories paint a picture of an AI industry scaling at unprecedented speed, with hidden financials, massive user adoption, and a race for the best learning resources.
editorial.body: The WSJ's revelation of $3T in off-balance-sheet spending underscores that the AI investment race is far bigger than reported [1]. Meanwhile, Slack's new Code and Claude Academy show that companies are betting on collaboration and education to lock in users. And with Codex hitting 20 million users, AI's role in programming is now mainstream—but the demand may outpace compute capacity.
editorial.pull_quote: The real battle isn't just about who builds the best model—it's who can turn that model into an essential tool for millions of workers.
editorial.outro: As AI spending, adoption, and training all accelerate, expect more scrutiny on financial disclosures and compute scalability in the coming months.

takeaway.label: IF YOU TAKE ONE THING FROM THIS
takeaway.text: For decision-makers: stay alert to hidden AI costs and invest in training your team on the tools that are becoming industry standards, like Claude Academy and Slack Code.
